model.title: Model reached through its API
model.applies_to: A foundation model called directly: a new model or a new version, with no harness and no application around it.
ask: Which system prompt, if any, will callers use, and who writes it?
Are image, audio or file inputs enabled?
Will callers attach tools, and which?
Is the identifier pinned to a dated version?

threats.why: The baseline: what it does when asked plainly.
Read beside every refusal figure; a model that refuses everything scores perfectly on misuse.
The gap between the plain rate and the rate under a jailbreak is the uplift.
Applies as soon as callers pass documents or other content with the request.
Safeguards are usually tuned on plain English text.
Only if image input is enabled.
Callers put rules and sometimes secrets in system prompts.
Anything placed in context can be asked for.
Matters most for models fine-tuned on the organisation's data.
If the model will write code.
If callers attach tools.
If callers attach tools and persistent memory.
A bare-API result does not describe the model inside a product or harness.
Capability, not resistance: a different question from the rest of this list.
Relevant when output is acted on without checking.
Open weights only: the artefact itself can be the attack.
Cannot be tested from outside; vendor statements are the only evidence.
Per-request cost and rate limits.
What the vendor keeps and where.
Aliases move; results describe one version.

agent-in-harness.title: Model inside an agent harness
agent-in-harness.applies_to: A model driving a coding, desktop or command-line agent that reads files and tool results and takes actions.
ask: Which harness and version, and does it update itself?
Which tools are on, and which need approval?
What can the agent reach from where it runs: credentials, network, other repositories?
Which content does it read that an outsider can write?
Are provider safeguards on in this harness, and does the harness add its own?

threats.why: The reason this template exists: results on the bare API do not transfer to the harness, in either direction.
Every file, issue, web page and tool result the agent reads is an instruction channel.
Shell, file and network tools turn a steered model into actions.
Environment variables, credentials and source code are within reach of tools that can send data.
The agent runs with the user's credentials unless scoped otherwise.
The agent runs code by design; what matters is where.
Refusal of malicious tasks, measured inside the harness.
Completion of legitimate and dual-use tasks, read beside refusal.
Harness system prompts and tool framing change what gets through.
For coding agents: the security of what is written.
If the harness keeps memory or instruction files between sessions.
Skills, plugins, rule files and MCP servers added to the harness.
Open weights only.
Approval prompts are the main safeguard in most harnesses.
If the agent's output feeds automation such as CI or other agents.
Long unattended runs with standing access.
An agent with a shell is closer to operational capability than a chat model.
Loops and long runs.
Source code and tool output leave the machine.
Model alias and harness version both move.

app.title: Application built on a model
app.applies_to: Something the organisation or a supplier built: a chat assistant, a retrieval application, a workflow with a model in it.
ask: Who are the users, and are any of them outside the organisation?
What does the application retrieve or load into the prompt, and who can write to those sources?
What does the application do with the model's output?
Which defences are the application's own, and can each be switched off for a comparison run?

threats.why: User input and retrieved content share the prompt with the application's instructions.
The application's users will try.
What the application will help with under the organisation's name.
Defences that block legitimate users.
The application's prompt is its configuration.
Other users' data, retrieved documents and secrets in context.
If anything retrieved can be written by someone else.
Where the reply is rendered, stored or executed.
If the application has tools.
If the application has tools that change something.
The application's service account usually sees more than any one user should.
If history or memory is stored.
Filters in front of the model are often text-pattern based.
If users act on answers.
Plugins and connectors the application loads.
Public endpoints with per-token cost.
The application's own logs and the model vendor's.
Model upgrades behind an unchanged application.

decision-model.title: Decision model
decision-model.applies_to: A model that takes a state and typed questions with a closed answer set and returns answers with probabilities, used to route, gate, grade or screen.

core_benchmark.note: Run it first. Its references/threat-model.md says where the risks come from for this subject type and lists the core threats it measures in two lanes (published benchmarks and its own core set); its scorecard compares models threat by threat. The threats below are the wider review list, including those no benchmark measures.

ask: What does the decision gate, and what happens on each answer?
Who writes the question instructions and option criteria, and is any of that text built from data?
Who controls the content being judged?
Is there an abstain option, and what does the caller do on refusal or error?
Is a confidence threshold used, and what happens below it?
Which wire format: one undifferentiated state, or separate roles?

threats.why: Start here: decide which error is which before reading any number.
The judged content is usually attacker-controlled and arrives as one blob.
Labels and criteria are prompt.
First-option bias and wording sensitivity are documented by vendors.
Decides whether 'escalate when unsure' works.
Every response returns a signal.
A model that must answer will.
When the model approves an agent's tool calls.
Audit rests on logging.
Encoding, language and image overlays.
No seed; aliases move.
Input-token billing with very large contexts and many questions per request.
Limited to probing through probabilities.
When decisions concern people.
The judged content is often the sensitive part.
Open-weight decision models only.

voice-model.title: Voice or realtime speech model
voice-model.applies_to: A speech-to-speech or realtime audio model, on a phone line, in an app or in a device.

core_benchmark.note: Run it first. Its references/threat-model.md says where the risks come from for this subject type and lists the core threats it measures in two lanes (published benchmarks and its own core set); its scorecard compares models threat by threat. The threats below are the wider review list, including those no benchmark measures.

ask: Where does audio come from: a phone line, a browser, a device in a room?
Who else can be heard on the channel?
Which tools can a spoken request trigger?
Do any guardrails read a transcript rather than the audio?
How is the caller identified?
Is there a cap on session length and cost?

threats.why: The audio channel has been measured as weaker than text.
Real callers and attackers both vary the audio.
Anything audible is input.
If spoken requests can trigger tools.
If any safeguard works on a transcript.
Realtime turn-taking is part of the attack surface.
Voice is not authentication.
If the model can produce arbitrary voices.
The text baseline the audio channel is compared with.
Legitimate callers refused, including by accent or noise.
Through any text or documents the voice agent is given.
Spoken extraction of the agent's instructions.
Account data read aloud to the wrong caller.
Realtime sessions bill by the minute.
Recordings and transcripts.
Realtime model aliases.

image-model.title: Image generation or editing model
image-model.applies_to: A model that produces or edits images from text or from other images. For image input to a chat model, use the model template and vision-model-benchmark.

core_benchmark.note: Run it first. Its references/threat-model.md says where the risks come from for this subject type and lists the core threats it measures in two lanes (published benchmarks and its own core set); its scorecard compares models threat by threat. The threats below are the wider review list, including those no benchmark measures.

ask: Who can prompt it, and where do the outputs go?
Does it accept reference or input images?
What does the organisation's content policy prohibit?
Does the vendor document provenance metadata or a watermark?

threats.why: No standardised benchmark exists for this.
Impersonation and non-consensual imagery.
Whether an output can later be identified as generated.
If the model edits or is conditioned on input images.
Prompt rewording against the content filter.
Benign prompts blocked by the content filter.
Reproduction of training images.
Open-weight image models and their add-on weights.
Generation is expensive per request.
Uploaded reference images, especially of people.
Filter and model updates.

feature.title: New agent feature
feature.applies_to: One capability being switched on in an agent the organisation already runs. The plan lists the threats for the feature named in review.json (subject.feature) plus the common ones.

guided_review.note: A guided review skill with one threat-and-test template per feature type. Use it for the threats below that no benchmark measures; it writes evidence rows.

ask: What can the agent do with the feature on that it could not do before?
Which new content does it read, and who can write it?
Which new credentials or sessions does it use?
Can the feature be limited to some users, sites, tools or data first?

common.why: A new feature usually arrives with new scopes.
New data leaves the organisation with each feature.
Features change behind a flag without a version.

computer-use.why: Everything on screen is input: pages, pop-ups, documents, notifications.
Clicks and keystrokes can do anything the logged-in user can.
Screen content and open sessions are within reach.
Watching an agent click is not reviewing it.

memory.why: What one session stores another can read.
Memory holds what users said earlier.

connectors.why: Each connector or MCP server is third-party code and third-party text.
Connected data sources others can write to.
A connector that can send is a route out.

code-execution.why: The feature is code execution; the question is its reach.
Files and network reachable from the sandbox.
Code that is kept after the session.

multi-agent.why: One steered agent steers the rest.
Harder to see which agent did what.
Injection reaches every agent that reads the shared content.

background-agent.why: Runs start with no person present.
Output goes straight into other systems.
Nobody is watching the content it reads.
